shortIntro: The capital region — best infrastructure, but the toughest visa income threshold. Includes Seoul and Incheon.
longIntro: Gyeonggi-do wraps around Seoul and Incheon, giving digital nomads the country's densest transit network, fastest internet, and largest coworking scene. It's the capital-tier region for visa purposes, so the income bar is highest — except in a handful of population-decline-designated counties (see the region page for details), which qualify at the lower non-capital threshold.

shortIntro: A good match for outdoor activity lovers, with snowy mountains and beaches for surfing.
longIntro: Gangwon-do is the Korean region with both the highest density of mountains and plenty of beaches. That makes it especially suitable for those who prefer outdoor activities — hiking, surfing and winter sports — over big city vibes. Gangneung is also known for its strong coffee culture and sea-view cafes.

Reachable within a few hours from the capital region, it's a popular leisure destination for Koreans, so expect it to get more crowded on weekends and public holidays. Developed coworking spaces are rare, but every city has plenty of study cafés that offer quite similar facilities.

shortIntro: Central and well-connected — an easy KTX ride from Seoul without capital-area prices or thresholds.
longIntro: Covering Chungcheongbuk-do, Chungcheongnam-do, Daejeon, and Sejong, this region sits at Korea's geographic center with strong KTX rail links to both Seoul and the south. Daejeon's research-institute density gives it a quietly technical, unpretentious feel — good for nomads who want short trips to the capital without living (or paying) there.

shortIntro: Korea's biggest non-capital cities — Busan, Daegu, Ulsan — plus historic Gyeongju and quiet coastal towns.
longIntro: Gyeongsangbuk-do, Gyeongsangnam-do, Busan, Daegu, and Ulsan give this region the widest range of any non-capital area: a genuine second-city nomad scene in Busan, ancient temples and tombs around Gyeongju, and industrial-turned-creative pockets in Daegu. Non-capital visa thresholds apply throughout.

shortIntro: Korea's food capital region — Jeonju and Gwangju anchor a slower, flavor-forward southwest.
longIntro: Jeollabuk-do, Jeollanam-do, and Gwangju are widely considered the heart of Korean cuisine, and the pace here matches: fewer crowds, lower costs, and a strong sense of place. Some of the lowest population density outside Gangwon, which also means some of the most population-decline-support-eligible counties in the country.

shortIntro: Korea's original workation island — volcanic coastline, and the country's most established remote-work culture.
longIntro: Jeju-do has the longest track record as a Korean remote-work destination, with coworking spaces and month-long-stay guesthouses concentrated around Jeju City and Seogwipo. Island living means higher import costs than the mainland non-capital average, offset by direct flights from Seoul and a mature short/medium-term rental market.
